cases.title: terminal: reflow capacity adjustment should use current page

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
While reflowing, if we required more page capacity, we were using `cap.<field> * 2` to grow the capacity. But `cap` references the _source page capacity_. What this means is that for _every single row_ we would hit our capacity limit again and call `adjustCapacity` again, since we were never actually increasing our capacity to begin with.

This commit replaces our capacity growth by using our current target page capacity as the source instead. Under edge case scenarios, this reduces the `adjustCapacity` burden and should result in performance improvements.

cases.title: Introduce Tripwire to test errdefer and fix some found issues

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
This adds a new single-file library called "Tripwire" in `src/tripwire.zig`. This library helps inject failures around `try` cases for the purpose of testing `errdefer`. It is fully optimized away in non-test builds (even debug), turning into zero space and zero assembly. 

From this, I've verified (via unit tests w/ tripwire) and fixed a number of errdefer issues:

* PageList init with non-standard pages that requires more than 1 page can leak on allocation error on the 2nd+ loop
* Tabstop allocation failure on resize corrupts the internal state (invalid cols)
* `Screen.selectionString` would leak memory on late allocation failures
* Screen search could leak memory on late allocation failures
* `SharedGrid.renderGlyph` in our font subsystem would corrupt the glyph cache if failure occurred
* `SharedGrid.init` could leak memory if loading font metrics failed

In addition to the bugs found, there is now tripwire coverage around more of our core and we should continue to add more. I've also added significantly more explicit error sets as I found them.

**AI disclosure:** AI wrote some of the tests, but tripwire itself is all handwritten and everything was reviewed.

cases.title: feat(macos): add SSH image paste support

label.rationale: Filled Generated-by or AI checkbox. Disclosure is not a fail label.

cases.body:
Closes #10516

## Summary

When pasting an image from the clipboard while in an SSH session, Ghostty now automatically uploads the image to the remote host via SCP and inserts the remote file path instead.

This enables seamless image sharing with remote tools like Claude Code that can read local files but not the local clipboard.

## How it works

1. User copies image to clipboard
2. User presses Ctrl+V in SSH session  
3. Ghostty detects image data + finds active SSH ControlMaster socket
4. Image uploads via SCP to `/tmp/ghostty-paste-{uuid}.png` on remote
5. Remote path is inserted as text

Uses existing SSH ControlMaster sockets for authentication - no password prompts.

## Changes

- `macos/Sources/Helpers/SSHImagePaste.swift` - Core upload logic (280 lines)
- `macos/Sources/Helpers/Extensions/NSPasteboard+Extension.swift` - Image detection
- `macos/Sources/Ghostty/Ghostty.App.swift` - Integration in clipboard handling
- `src/config/Config.zig` - Config options

## Config options

```
ssh-image-paste = true          # Enable/disable feature (default: true)
ssh-image-paste-path = /tmp     # Remote upload directory (default: /tmp)
```

## Test plan

- [x] Copy image to clipboard, paste in SSH session → path appears
- [x] Paste text in SSH session → normal behavior
- [x] Paste when not in SSH → graceful fallback
- [x] Works with Claude Code on remote host

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

cases.body: Fixes #9932; also see https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/9930. **Submitting this as a draft PR to get feedback on the areas listed below. Please let me know whether this is going in the right direction.** - The code was largely written by Claude Code, with guidance from me. I have read through the implementation and reviewed it; overall, the code looks reasonable to me. (I have of course also checked that it actually works; see below.) I have also improved the factoring and removed some unnecessary duplication etc., especially on the Swift side. - I have read the contribution guidelines and AI policy, but it still leaves room for interpretation (e.g. with regards to how many comments are "too much" etc., see below); happy to make adjustments to bring this further in line with your expectations. Again, this is just a rough first draft. - I have intentionally left in most comments (and asked Claude to focus on the _motivation_ of the code); happy to clean them up further if you find them too verbose. - Caveat: I have hardly any experience with Zig, so I may have missed something in that implementation. In particular, my knowledge of PinMap is limited, so please feel free to provide some guidance there (see below). - Speaking of PinMap, I am unsure how inefficient the current implementation is in practice. But even if it is somewhat inefficient, it could serve as a starting point for a more efficient implementation as needed in practice. - To my understanding, we could also replace `cachedScreenContents` and `cachedVisibleContents` with accesses into the `cachedScreenTextInfo`; I also don't think they are accessed much more frequently than the `cachedScreenTextInfo`, so any possible performance overhead of `cachedScreenTextInfo` would probably be tolerable. Happy to make these changes, let me know. - Speaking of `cachedVisibleContents`, I am unsure why reading the visible text with `ghostty_surface_read_text` would be less expensive (potentially by not requiring a PinMap, but how?) than getting byte offsets into the entire text using a PinMap. - As an alternative, maybe we could include a pointer to a PinMap itself in the `cachedScreenTextInfo` struct and cache that, to minimize the frequency of recreating PinMaps for Accessibility methods? That could be worthwhile to also optimize the other AX methods (e.g. for getting the rectangles of certain characters etc.). We would probably need to manage the PinMap's lifetime in Swift, but I guess that's doable. - @mitchellh your feedback on how we should best architect this aspect, both from a caching and a Swift/Zig interop perspective, would be greatly appreciated. - Tests are only on the Zig layer right now; having good tests on the Swift layer might be a bit more difficult because we'd need to test them in the UI harness (haven't looked too much into that yet). - Not _all_ Accessibility methods have been implemented yet, but hopefully a subset that already provides value; most others (e.g. selected text range, notifications for that) would add slightly less value and I already feel like this PR is getting large enough. - As Accessibility implementations also very much depend on how AX clients actually interact with this API (and what they expect from it), it would be useful to get feedback from actual users of AX clients. /cc @grishy @burakssen - For reference, I did use my own app [Cotypist](https://cotypist.app) (which also uses AX extensively) to see whether the implementation is sufficient for it. Will attach a screenshot of the result shortly; overall, it looks decent, but there's room for improvement. But I felt it was good to first get some feedback on the current state. - Screenshot: Completions are shown in roughly the right location: - `macos/tools/check-accessibility/` tool: Pure AI slop, but very useful for debugging/verifying the implementation; happy to remove it from the PR before leaving draft status; let me know. --- _AI slop (but guided by me in an attempt to make it actually useful) follows_ # PR: Implement rich macOS accessibility for terminal surfaces ## Overview Adds comprehensive macOS Accessibility support so VoiceOver and other assistive technologies can read terminal content, navigate by line, locate characters spatially, and stay in sync as new output arrives. The implementation spans the full stack: Zig core terminal logic, the C API bridge, and the Swift/AppKit accessibility overrides. All positional data flows as **UTF-8 byte offsets** from the Zig core. The Swift layer converts to/from **UTF-16 code units** (NSRange semantics) at the boundary, since every macOS Accessibility API speaks NSRange. ## Accessibility functions | Override | Purpose | How it works | |---|---|---| | `accessibilityValue` | Full terminal text (scrollback + active) | Reads from `ScreenTextInfo` cache, which calls `ghostty_surface_ax_text` to get text + viewport byte range via the Zig pin map | | `accessibilityNumberOfCharacters` | Total character count | `NSString.length` (UTF-16 code units) on the cached text | | `accessibilityVisibleCharacterRange` | Viewport range within the full text | Zig core walks its pin map to find viewport start/end byte offsets; Swift converts to an NSRange via `String.Index` | | `accessibilityLine(for:)` | Line number for a UTF-16 character index | Converts the UTF-16 index to a `String.Index`, slices, counts newlines | | `accessibilityRange(forLine:)` | Character range for a line number | Walks UTF-16 code units via `NSString.character(at:)` counting `\n` boundaries | | `accessibilityInsertionPointLineNumber` | Cursor's line number | Gets cursor byte offset from Zig (`ax_cursor_offset`), counts `0x0A` bytes directly in UTF-8 — safe because no multi-byte sequence contains `0x0A` | | `accessibilityFrame(for:)` | Screen-coordinate bounds of a character range (AXBoundsForRange) | Converts NSRange → UTF-8 byte offset, asks Zig for cell bounds, flips Y from top-left to AppKit bottom-left, converts view → screen coords. Same-line ranges get a tight rect; multi-line ranges use full view width (matching NSTextView/Terminal.app behavior) | | `accessibilityRange(for:)` | Character at a screen point (AXRangeForPosition) | Converts screen → window → view → flipped-Y coordinates, asks Zig for the byte offset at that grid position, converts back to a 1-character NSRange | | `accessibilityContentDidChange` | Notifies VoiceOver of new output | Invalidates the text cache and posts `NSAccessibility.valueChanged`. Triggered by a push-based `content_changed` action from the renderer — no polling | ## Changes by layer ### Zig core — `src/terminal/Screen.zig` New `AccessibilityText` and `AccessibilityCell` types, plus four functions: - **`accessibilityText`** — Builds a full-screen selection, generates text with a `PinMap`, then scans the map to find the viewport's start/end byte offsets using a node-to-row-offset hash map. - **`accessibilityGridForOffset`** — Resolves a byte offset to a viewport-relative `(col, row)` cell via the pin map. Returns `null` for offsets in scrollback above the viewport. - **`accessibilityOffsetForGrid`** — Inverse: resolves viewport `(col, row)` to a byte offset. Falls back to row-start if the exact column has no content (e.g. cursor past end of line). - **`accessibilityCursorOffset`** — Convenience wrapper that calls `accessibilityOffsetForGrid` with the current cursor coordinates. Includes 17 unit tests covering scrollback, wide characters, soft wraps, empty screens, round-trips, and edge cases. ### Surface — `src/Surface.zig` Thin wrappers that lock the renderer mutex and delegate to `Screen`. `boundsForOffset` also handles content-scale conversion (pixels ↔ points) and wide-character cell widths. ### C API — `include/ghostty.h`, `src/apprt/embedded.zig` Five new exports: - `ghostty_surface_ax_text` / `_ax_text_free` — text + viewport byte range - `ghostty_surface_ax_bounds` — byte offset → view-local cell rect - `ghostty_surface_ax_offset` — view-local point → byte offset - `ghostty_surface_ax_cursor_offset` — cursor byte offset New `ghostty_ax_text_s` and `ghostty_ax_bounds_s` structs. All offsets are UTF-8 bytes; the docstrings note that platform layers using NSRange must convert. ### Action / Message — `src/apprt/action.zig`, `src/apprt/surface.zig` New `content_changed` action and surface message, replacing the previous polling approach. ### Renderer — `src/renderer/generic.zig` When the terminal's dirty flag is set, pushes a `content_changed` message through the surface mailbox (instant/non-blocking, like the scrollbar notification). ### Swift / macOS — `SurfaceView_AppKit.swift`, `Ghostty.App.swift` - New `ScreenTextInfo` struct with `viewportRange` (NSRange), `utf16Length`, `utf8Offset(of:)`, and `characterIndex(forUTF8Offset:)` helpers. - Separate `cachedScreenTextInfo` cache (500ms TTL) — kept distinct from `cachedScreenContents` because the pin-map-based text generation is more expensive and only needed by accessibility callers. - `CachedValue` gains an `invalidate()` method for push-based cache busting. - `Ghostty.App` dispatches the `content_changed` action to `surfaceView.accessibilityContentDidChange()`. ### Test tool — `macos/tools/check-accessibility/` Standalone Swift Package Manager CLI that queries a running Ghostty instance via the macOS AX API. Dumps all text-area attributes and parameterized attributes (bounds, ranges, line navigation), runs automated consistency checks, and supports `--listen` mode for monitoring `valueChanged`/`selectedTextChanged` notifications in real time.

cases.title: Add swap_split action to exchange terminal content between panes

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
## Summary

  Adds a new `swap_split` action that exchanges the terminal content of the currently focused split with the neighbor split in a given direction. Unlike `goto_split` (which moves focus), `swap_split`
  preserves the tree layout and split ratios — only the two leaf views trade places. Useful for rearranging panes without reshaping the layout.

  Example: with a big left pane and a small right pane, pressing the swap binding with direction `right` puts the left pane's content in the small right position and vice versa. Pane sizes are unchanged.

  ## Default keybinds

  - **macOS**: `Cmd+Shift+Option+Arrow` (mirrors the existing `Cmd+Option+Arrow` for `goto_split`)
  - **Linux/GTK**: `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Arrow` (mirrors the existing `Ctrl+Alt+Arrow` for `goto_split`)

  Both are marked `performable`, so at a layout edge with no neighbor in that direction the action is a no-op and the key passes through.

  ## Implementation

  - **Action** (`src/apprt/action.zig`): new `swap_split: GotoSplit` variant. `GHOSTTY_ACTION_SWAP_SPLIT` appended at the end of the C enum to avoid renumbering existing values.
  - **Binding** (`src/input/Binding.zig`): `swap_split: SplitFocusDirection`. Command palette entries added in `src/input/command.zig`.
  - **Surface dispatch** (`src/Surface.zig`): mirrors the `goto_split` arm.
  - **Core SplitTree** (`src/datastruct/split_tree.zig`): new `pub fn swap(gpa, a, b)` — clones the tree and swaps the two leaf view pointers in place (same `@constCast` pattern as `resizeInPlace`). Zoomed
  handle is preserved (zoom tracks position).
  - **GTK apprt**: `swap(to)` wrapper on `split_tree.zig` reusing `goto` for target resolution; `swapSplit` handler in `application.zig`.
  - **macOS Swift SplitTree**: new `swapping(_:with:)` using `path(to:)` + two `replacingNode` calls. Clears zoom (matches `resizing`/`inserting`).
  - **macOS dispatch** (`Ghostty.App.swift`): `swapSplit` handler uses `replaceSurfaceTree(_, moveFocusTo:, moveFocusFrom:, undoAction: "Swap Split")`, so the operation integrates with the existing undo
  system. Focus follows the content (user's terminal moves with them).

  ## Tests

  - `src/datastruct/split_tree.zig`: two tests — swap preserves layout/ratios and swaps leaf views; swap-with-self is a no-op clone.
  - `macos/Tests/Splits/SplitTreeTests.swift`: three tests — leaf swap preserves direction/ratio, self-swap no-op, zoomed state cleared on swap.

  ## Known inconsistency (matches existing goto_split)

  GTK spatial navigation wraps at edges (`nearestWrapped`); macOS spatial navigation does not (`slots(in:from:)` strict directional). So `swap_split:right` from the rightmost pane wraps to leftmost on GTK
  but is a no-op on macOS. This matches the pre-existing `goto_split` behavior in both apprts and is not addressed in this PR.

cases.title: Sync middle-click paste with copy-on-select

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
Implements the behavior from #9788.

Today, middle-click paste always reads from the selection clipboard (or the
system clipboard on platforms without a selection clipboard). With this change
it follows `copy-on-select`:

- `true`: selection clipboard (unchanged)
- `clipboard`: system clipboard
- `false`: selection clipboard (also unchanged, preserves traditional X11
  middle-click behavior)

The idea is symmetry: if `copy-on-select = clipboard` writes selections to the
system clipboard, middle-click should come back from there too.

Also updated the config doc comment, which previously claimed middle-click
"will always use the selection clipboard".

### Testing

`zig build test` passes locally (macOS, Zig 0.15.2).

I couldn't do interactive runtime testing. My local env currently can't produce
a working `Ghostty.app` because of a Zig 0.15.2 + Xcode 26.4 TBD linker bug
(upstream fix in zig PR #31673, not released yet). Marking draft so nobody
merges before someone checks the three copy-on-select modes on a real build.

cases.title: Add support for RTL languages

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
Before this change, multi-word Hebrew phrases rendered with each word's letters correctly reversed but the words themselves in logical (left-to-right) order. Typing "חדש שלום" produced "חדש" visually left of "שלום", whereas VS Code and the Unicode Bidi Algorithm put the first-typed word on the right.

The fix is a three-layer pipeline:

1. src/font/shaper/run.zig tags each TextRun with `right_to_left` (run contains a strong-RTL codepoint from Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, etc.) and `all_spaces` (run is entirely U+0020). The CoreText space-split rule already produces one run per word.

2. src/font/shaper/coretext.zig keeps the intra-run reversal that places cluster c at cell index `(run.cells - 1) - c`, so letters within a single Hebrew word render in RTL order.

3. src/renderer/generic.zig collects each row's runs into a row-local `RowRun` list and applies `reorderRtlBlocks` before the cell loop. A block is a maximal sequence of RTL runs plus the space runs flanked on both sides by RTL runs; leading or trailing spaces at an LTR boundary are not absorbed, and an LTR run between two RTL words splits them into separate blocks. Each block is reversed and the runs' offsets are reassigned so the block still spans the same columns.

A subtle constraint we hit: a TextRun yielded by RunIterator.next() is only shapeable until the next next() call, because the iterator hook's prepare() resets the shaper's codepoint buffer. rebuildRow therefore shapes each run at the moment it is yielded and copies the resulting cells into a row-local std.ArrayList(font.shape.Cell), so shape results survive both the reordering pass and the bounded shape cache.

Tests:

- New reorderRtlBlocks tests in generic.zig covering no-RTL, two adjacent RTL words, LTR prompt + RTL block, trailing space not absorbed, and LTR-between-RTL splitting.
- New shaper tests in coretext.zig: shape Hebrew string, shape mixed Hebrew and latin string, shape multiple Hebrew words, run iterator splits prompt from Hebrew phrase.
- Updated stale run-count expectations in shape nerd fonts and shape U+3C9 with JB Mono that were broken by the earlier space-split rule.

Known limitations: cursor, selection, and background fills still use logical column indices, so for RTL blocks they sit on the logical cell instead of where the glyph ended up. RTL detection is a codepoint-range heuristic, not full UBA. Arabic contextual shaping and wide characters inside RTL blocks are not exercised.

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
Part of preparation for adding a Win32 application runtime (discussion #2563). One of three small, independent build fixes that together unblock the Windows GNU-ABI library build.

On Windows with non-MSVC ABI, `pub const DllMain` resolved to `void` (a type), and Zig's stdlib `start.zig` then tried to call it as a function via `root.DllMain(...)`, failing to compile with "type 'type' not a function".

This restructures the conditional so MSVC keeps its existing CRT-init handler unchanged, non-MSVC Windows gets a no-op `BOOL` handler, and non-Windows continues to resolve to `void`.

Verified: `zig build -Dtarget=native-native-gnu -Dapp-runtime=none [-Doptimize=ReleaseSafe]` now builds cleanly on Windows.

cases.title: macOS: sync appearance after screen parameters change

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
In #5389 there are multiple reports of tab bars appearing incorrectly after disconnecting an external monitor when Ghostty is in fullscreen.

BaseTerminalController handles the notfiication from AppKit about a screen change and, for non-fullscreen windows, it calls setFrame, which triggers windowDidMove, which calls fixTabBar. But for fullscreen windows, none of this happens, we skip clamping because macOS handles the sizing and the tab bar doesn't get fixed.

I've restructured the handler so that the clamping is conditional on the window being non-fullscreen and window.screen being defined, and regardless of the clamping, called syncAppearance at the end of the handler.

This has fixed the issue for me, reproduced locally using BetterDisplay to create a virtual second display and with my external monitor.

AI disclosure: I used GLM 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 in OpenCode to investigate the issue and the call chain, but I fully understand what is going on and wrote this PR and my commit message and the comment and the code myself.

cases.title: gtk: improve split sizing

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
This PR improves the way splits/surfaces are sized in the GTK app, which eliminates flickering and slightly improves performance.

Fixes #13328, #12709, #11187.
Related #8208 (closed) but some later comments mention flickering issues persisting.
Builds on top of the changes in #12698.

Previously an idle callback was used to sync the split ratio between the GTK widget tree and the split tree data structure that represents the split layout. The widget tree contains a `SplitTreeSplit` widget, which wraps a `GtkPaned` widget, for every split. During size allocation a `GtkPaned` widget first computes the initial position of the divider and thereby the size for its two children. We get notified of that position (and the max possible position) via the `propPosition/propMaxPosition` callbacks in `SplitTreeSplit` and set up an idle callback (the `onIdle` function) to update the position if it does not match the desired split ratio. Since the initial position is often not correct, especially in nested layouts or if the ratio is not 0.5, a surface will first be shown with the wrong size for a few frames until the idle callback runs and corrects the sizing. In nested layouts it might take multiple rounds of size allocation and idle callbacks until every surface gets the correct size. This causes flickering as widgets eventually snap to another size, which is especially noticeable if the layout changes quickly e.g. when resizing a split using keybinds.

To fix this, the divider position will now be corrected directly from the `propMaxPosition` callback, which runs during GTK size allocation, right after a `GtkPaned` computes the initial position and right before it uses the position to allocate sizes for its two children. With this change every surface will be sized correctly during the first round of size allocation. 
 The idle callback is still used to update the ratio in the split tree when a split is resized by manually dragging the divider in the UI. The logic to sync the split ratio was moved to the new `syncSplitRatio` function which is called from both `propMaxPosition` and `onIdle`.

This is kind of hacky, but I reviewed the GTK source code in detail to verify that this is safe (see the various code comments for more details). I also tested extensively on both Hyprland and KDE Plasma: creating deeply nested layouts, resizing with both keybinds and dragging dividers by hand, with multiple tabs, resizing the entire window, resizing entire subtrees to 0 and back. Everything seems to work fine.

For performance testing I used sysprof which can also collect GTK stats. When creating/deleting/resizing splits I can measure a slight but consistent increase in GTK FPS (+5 to 10) on my system. Other than that CPU usage and FPS seem to be the same before and after. I guess this makes sense, while we added a bit of work to the GTK loop during size allocation, we avoid surfaces being resized.

For the flickering, here's a side-by-side comparison. Left is before the changes, right is after.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2a4f0b4b-e113-49b5-b0d7-d9e507a5a4ff

cases.title: surface: resolve punctuation in clicked file paths

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

Command-click path matches can include trailing sentence punctuation or a following prose word, such as `SKILL.md again.`. The opener then receives a path that doesn't exist.

Trimming punctuation blindly isn't safe, because `.`, `;`, `?`, and `!` can all be valid filename endings on macOS. So the resolver now checks the exact accessible path first. cases.title: macos: show which clause is being converted while typing Japanese

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body: This PR is about how Ghostty displays Japanese text while it is being converted, which I raised in discussion #14737. When I type Japanese, the input method first shows the text I typed as text that is not yet committed. In this PR, I call it the composing text. The input method splits the composing text into clauses (short groups of words) and converts one clause at a time. The input method sends the composing text to Ghostty with two kinds of underline attributes: a thin underline for the whole composing text and a thick underline for the clause being converted. Ghostty discards these underline attributes and draws one thin underline under the whole composing text. Because of this, I cannot see which clause will change when I press the space key or the arrow keys. With this PR, Ghostty keeps the underline attributes. Ghostty draws the clause being converted with a thick underline and the rest of the composing text with a dotted underline. This PR does not add a configuration option. When no clause is marked, Ghostty displays the composing text the same way as before. This includes text that is still being typed as kana: Apple's Japanese input method puts a thick underline under all of that text, so a thick underline under the whole composing text is not treated as a clause. ### Screenshots In both screenshots, the composing text is 今日はいい天気です ("It is nice weather today"), and the clause being converted is いい ("nice"). This PR (a dotted underline for the composing text and a thick underline for the clause being converted): Another option that I tried (a thin underline for the composing text and a thick underline for the clause being converted): With the thin underline and the thick underline, the difference is hard to see. Personally, I found the combination of the dotted underline and the thick underline easier to read, so I chose the dotted underline. If you prefer the thin underline, the change is one line in the function `addPreeditCell` in `src/renderer/generic.zig`. ### Changes - macOS app (`SurfaceView_AppKit.swift`): `validAttributesForMarkedText` returns `[.underlineStyle]`, so AppKit no longer removes the underline attributes. The macOS app finds the range with the thick underline and passes the range to the Ghostty core through a new C API function, `ghostty_surface_preedit_selected`. The existing function `ghostty_surface_preedit` does not change. - Ghostty core (`Surface.zig`, `renderer/State.zig`): each codepoint of the composing text gets a `selected` flag that is true when the codepoint is in the clause being converted. - Renderer (`renderer/generic.zig`): when the composing text has a clause being converted, the renderer draws that clause with a new `underline_thick` sprite and the other codepoints with the existing `underline_dotted` sprite. - Linux version (GTK): the GTK code passes no range, so the GTK version does not change. - Tests (`SurfaceViewAppKitTests.swift`): new cases check the range that the macOS app finds, for example a clause after an emoji, a double underline, and a thick underline under the whole text. ### Testing - All Ghostty tests (`zig build test -Dxcframework-target=native`), including the macOS app tests, pass on the current `main`. - On macOS 27.0.1, Claude Code built the app and used a script to type Japanese in a Ghostty window with Apple's Japanese input method and with one other Japanese input method, and took screenshots. It checked typing kana, converting, moving between clauses, changing the length of a clause, going back to kana, committing, a single clause, and composing text that is wider than the window. - It also typed with Apple's Korean (2-Set) and Chinese (Pinyin) input methods. They do not use a thick underline, and their composing text looks the same as before. - Finally, I typed Japanese in the built app myself and confirmed that the clause being converted has a thick underline and the rest has a dotted underline. ### AI disclosure I am not a developer, and my native language is Japanese. I used Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) for this PR. I decided what to change and how it should look. Claude Code read the Ghostty code to find the cause, wrote the code and the tests, ran the tests, and took the screenshots with a script. Claude Code also wrote the English of this text, and I checked it with Google Translate.

cases.body:
Labels every link in the viewport with a short key sequence, similar to Alacritty's hints. Typing a label acts on that link; escape cancels and backspace undoes a key. Hint mode is modal and swallows other keys.

The action takes a mode: `open`, `persist` (stay in hint mode after opening), or `copy` (copy the link to the clipboard). The label alphabet and colors are configurable via `hint-alphabet` and the `hint-*` color options.

Hint mode ends on wheel scroll or a config reload, since the labels would no longer line up with the text. A hint-alphabet with duplicate or non-printable characters is rejected with a warning.

Labels are drawn into the renderer's copy of the cells so clearing them just dirties the terminal.

cases.title: libghostty-vt: reject OSC 7501 reports with disallowed bytes in an id

label.rationale: Closed without merge. Population sample, not a slop label.

cases.body:
The report validator read ids through a ValueIterator filtered by the value alphabet, which skips a value containing any other byte. An id like `a@b` therefore looked absent instead of invalid, and the report fell back to the root record; with state=clear that removed every record, the outcome the parser's documentation says an invalid id must never have.

Validate every value without the filter, so the checks themselves reject bad bytes. The same filter also let a title or msg that isn't base64, an over-long value, or an unknown state slip through as a skipped pair rather than discarding the report, and those are fixed alongside. Anything that passes validation is within the alphabet, so readOption's filtered reads see the same values.

Fixes #14790

cases.title: build: add -Dinstalled-exe-path for the Linux launcher files

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
The Zig 0.17 port replaced the absolute path to the executable in the desktop file, D-Bus services and systemd user service with a bare  `ghostty`, since the install prefix is no longer known while the build  is configured. systemd resolves a bare ExecStart= name against a fixed search path rather than PATH: /usr/bin and /usr/local/bin on most systems, and only systemd's own directory on NixOS. So the service failed to start for any install outside those directories, including every Nix one.
    
-Dinstalled-exe-path gives the absolute path to write into those files. Without it they still name the executable alone, which is right for packages installing to /usr. The Nix package passes its output path, and the Flatpak manifests pass /app/bin/ghostty, which is what they produced before the port.

Fixes #14805

cases.title: kitty graphics: non-chunk continuations end the chunked transmission

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
While a chunked Kitty graphics load was in progress, every transmit or animation frame command was treated as its next chunk, regardless of its transmission medium. A file (`t=f`), temporary file (`t=t`), or shared memory (`t=s`) command arriving mid-load had its encoded path appended to the partial image as pixel data.

This diverged from Kitty. The spec only defines chunking for direct data, and continuation chunks must carry only the `m` and `q` keys, so a command with another medium can never be a continuation. Kitty abandons the in-progress load and handles the command as a new transmission, for both image and animation frame loads. A client that interrupts a load this way now gets the image or frame it asked for instead of a corrupted or failed one.

`execute` now destroys the in-progress load before dispatching any non-direct transmit or frame command, so the command is handled as a fresh transmission, including its own `q` setting.

cases.title: terminal: discard cancelled or aborted APC commands

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
ECMA-48 says a control string that is cancelled or aborted is thrown away. xterm only dispatches a control string on ST, and Kitty only ends an APC on ST or BEL, so neither runs the command.

https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-48/

cases.title: terminal: continuations must restart at C1 sequence introducers

label.rationale: Merged, no filled disclosure, no slop language, no hard markers.

cases.body:
A stream continuation that ended after an 8-bit C1 introducer had aborted an APC could not be exported. For example, `ESC _ data 0x9B` ends the APC and starts a CSI, but the tracker only treats ESC as the start of a new sequence, so it kept the aborted APC. Replaying that would end the APC a second time, and validation rejected it.

Export now starts at the last C1 introducer that moved the parser into a new sequence and writes it in its 7-bit ESC form.
